body.x: If you have been invited to a Shia wedding, are marrying into a Shia family, or are simply curious, the first thing to know is that a Shia marriage has two layers: a short, solemn contract ceremony that makes the couple married in the eyes of God, and the celebration that surrounds it. The contract — the nikah — can take less than half an hour. Everything else, the clothes, the food, the photography, is culture. This guide explains the contract itself: the words spoken, the people involved, and the questions outsiders most often ask.
First, the words: nikah, aqd and rishta

Nikah is the Arabic word for the marriage contract itself, and by extension for the ceremony at which it is concluded. The contract is also called the aqd, from an Arabic word for a knot or bond — the tying of two lives together. You may also hear rishta, an Urdu and Hindi word used across South Asian communities for a match or proposal: the search that leads to the nikah. Shia Islam is the tradition followed by a significant minority of the world's Muslims, with large communities in Iran, Iraq, Lebanon, Bahrain, Pakistan and India and a wide diaspora beyond them, and its marriage law rests on the Quran and the teachings of the Prophet Muhammad and the Imams of his household.
The heart of it: offer and acceptance

A Shia nikah becomes binding through a spoken formula called the sigha: an offer (ijab) and an acceptance (qabul), recited in Arabic, in the past tense, in a single sitting. In plain terms, one side declares the marriage — that the bride is given in marriage to the groom for the agreed mahr — and the other side immediately accepts. The couple may recite the words themselves, but very commonly each appoints a representative, a wakil: the bride's representative speaks her side, the groom's speaks his, often with a scholar or reciter guiding the wording so nothing is missed. Once offer and acceptance are complete, the couple are husband and wife. There is no exchange of rings or personal vows; the contract is the moment.
The people in the room: wali, witnesses and family

Three roles matter. The wali is the bride's guardian, usually her father or paternal grandfather. For a woman marrying for the first time, the majority view among contemporary Shia scholars (marjas) is that her wali's permission is required for the marriage to be valid; scholars differ on some details and exceptions, which is why families check with their own marja. Witnesses are the second role: two upright witnesses are strongly recommended at the contract in Shia law and are present at virtually every real ceremony, though jurists discuss their exact status for a permanent marriage differently from Sunni schools, where witnesses are a strict condition. And consent sits underneath everything: both bride and groom must agree freely. A marriage forced on either party is not a valid marriage, and families treat the bride's genuine, unpressured yes as foundational.
Mahr: the gift written into the contract

Every nikah includes a mahr: a gift from the groom to the bride, agreed before the contract is recited and written into it. The Quran presents the mahr as the bride's own right, given to her directly — this is the theme of verse 4:4 — and it belongs to her alone: not to her parents, and not to the groom to reclaim. It can be money, gold, or something else of agreed value, and couples commonly divide it into a portion given at the time of the contract and a portion deferred. There is no fixed amount in Shia law; families set it by agreement, and many scholars encourage keeping it modest rather than turning it into a contest. Because the mahr forms part of the contract's wording, it must be settled before the sigha is recited — one reason the ceremony itself is short: the real negotiation happened earlier.
So is it a wedding? The ceremony and the celebration

Outsiders are often surprised by how quiet the aqd is. It may happen in a mosque or Islamic centre, a family home, or a hall, with a short sermon and Quran recitation before the contract, prayers after it, and sweets or dates shared to mark the moment. In many communities the bride and groom are in separate rooms or sections during the recitation, joined through their representatives; in others they sit together. The large celebration — the mehndi, the reception, the walima feast hosted after the marriage — is where the colour, music and hundreds of guests belong. In law, though, it is the few minutes of the aqd that marry the couple: two people who have had their nikah are husband and wife even if the party is months away.

Is a nikah the same as a legal marriage? Not automatically. Whether the religious ceremony is recognised by the state depends on the country; many couples also complete a civil registration, and in some places the officiant is licensed to do both at once.
Can a Shia marry a non-Shia? Shia scholars permit marriage with other Muslims within conditions that vary by marja and circumstance, while marriage outside Islam is far more restricted. Families ask their own marja about their specific case.
What is mut'ah? A fixed-term marriage contract that exists in Shia jurisprudence, distinct from the permanent nikah described here, with its own separate rules. Shia Rishta, for clarity, is a platform for permanent marriage only.
Do the couple meet before the nikah? In most families, yes — in structured, family-aware settings: meetings, conversations and questions, all before any commitment. The contract comes at the end of a search, not the beginning.
Why Arabic, if nobody speaks it? The formula's wording carries legal weight, so it is kept in the language of the tradition, with translation and explanation provided. Its meaning is never a secret from the couple.

If you are at the searching stage yourself, this is the destination every rishta conversation is quietly aimed at: a short, careful contract, spoken aloud, witnessed, and meant for life. Shia Rishta exists for the part that comes before — helping Shia families find one another with privacy, family involvement and conversations that open only on mutual interest, so that when the day of the aqd arrives, the agreement it seals has been built properly.

excerpt: A plain-language guide to the Shia nikah — the contract, the words that make it binding, the people involved, and how the quiet ceremony differs from the wedding celebration around it.
title: How do Shias get married? Nikah explained simply
